'''Paul Joseph Steinhardt''' (born December 25, 1952) is an American [[theoretical physicist]] whose principal research is in cosmology and condensed matter physics. He is currently the [[Albert Einstein Professorship in Science|Albert Einstein Professor in Science]] at [[Princeton University]], where he is on the faculty of both the Departments of Physics and of Astrophysical Sciences.<ref name="Brief Bio">{{cite web | url=http://www.physics.princeton.edu/~steinh/webbrief/ | title=Biographical Sketch: Prof. Paul J. Steinhardt | publisher=Department of Physics at Princeton University | access-date=January 29, 2019}}</ref>

Steinhardt is best known for his development of new theories of the origin, evolution and future of the universe. He is also well known for his exploration of a new form of matter, known as [[quasicrystal]]s, which were thought to exist only as man-made materials until he co-discovered the first known natural [[quasicrystal]] in a museum sample.<ref name="Natural Quasicrystals"/> He subsequently led a separate team that followed up that discovery with several more examples of natural [[quasicrystal]]s recovered from the wilds of the Kamchatka Peninsula in far eastern Russia. Several years later, he and collaborators reported the accidental synthesis of a previously unknown type of quasicrystal in the remnants of the first atomic bomb test on July 16, 1945, at Alamagordo, New Mexico.<ref name="Atomic" >{{cite journal | last1 = Bindi | first1 = Luca | last2 = Kolb | first2 =William  | last3 = Eby | first3 = G. Nelson  |last4 = Asimow | first4 = Paul D. |last5 = Wallace | first5 = Terry C. |last6 = Steinhardt | first6 = Paul J. | year = 2021 | title = Accidental synthesis of a previously unknown quasicrystal in the first atomic bomb test | journal = PNAS| volume = 118| issue = June 1, 2021 118 (22) e2101350118 | article-number = e2101350118| doi = 10.1073/pnas.2101350118| pmid = 34001665| pmc = 8179242 |bibcode = 2021PNAS..11801350B| doi-access = free }}</ref>

He has written two popular books on these topics. ''Endless Universe: Beyond the Big Bang (2007)'', co-authored with [[Neil Turok]], describes the early struggles in challenging the widely accepted [[Big Bang|big bang theory]] and the subsequent development of the bouncing or cyclic theories of the universe, which are currently being explored and tested.<ref name="Endless Universe">{{cite book |title=Endless Universe: beyond the Big Bang |first1=P.J. |last1=Steinhardt |first2=N.G. |last2=Turok |publisher=Doubleday |year=2007 |isbn=978-0-385-50964-0 |url-access=registration |url=https://archive.org/details/endlessuniverseb0000stei }}</ref> ''The Second Kind of Impossible: The Extraordinary Quest for a New Form of Matter (2019)'' recounts the story of quasicrystals from his invention of the concept with his then-student [[Dov Levine]], to his expedition to far eastern Russia to recover meteorite fragments containing natural quasicrystal grains formed billions of years ago.<ref name="The Second Kind of Impossible" >{{cite book |title=The Second Kind of Impossible |first1=P.J. |last1=Steinhardt |publisher=Simon & Schuster |year=2019 |isbn=978-1-4767-2992-3}}</ref>

==Education and career==

Born in 1952 to Helen and Charles Steinhardt, Paul Steinhardt is the second oldest of four children. He grew up in Miami, Florida, where he attended Coral Gables Senior High School while attending classes at a local university. Steinhardt received his Bachelor of Science in physics at [[Caltech]] in 1974, and his Ph.D. in physics at [[Harvard University]] in 1978 where his advisor was [[Sidney Coleman]].<ref name=mathgene/> He was a Junior Fellow in the [[Harvard Society of Fellows]] from 1978 to 1981. He rose from junior faculty to Mary Amanda Wood Professor at the [[University of Pennsylvania]] between 1981 and 1998, during which he maintained a long-term association with the [[Thomas J. Watson Research Center]], and has been on the faculty at [[Princeton University]] since the Fall of 1998. He co-founded the Princeton Center for Theoretical Science and served as its Director from 2007 to 2019.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://paulsteinhardt.org/bio/|title= Paul Steinhardt Bio|website=Paul Steinhardt|access-date=26 June 2019}}</ref>

==Research==
===Inflationary cosmology===
Beginning in the early 1980s, Steinhardt co-authored seminal papers that helped to lay the foundations of [[inflation (physics)|inflationary cosmology]].

====Slow-roll inflation and generation of the seeds for galaxies====
[[File:Paul Steinhardt University of Pennsylvania.jpg|thumb|left|Steinhardt at the [[University of Pennsylvania]]]]
In 1982, Steinhardt and [[Andreas Albrecht (cosmologist)|Andreas Albrecht]]<ref name="journals.aps.org">{{cite journal | last1 = Albrecht | first1 = A. | last2 = Steinhardt | first2 = P. J. | year = 1982 | title = Cosmology For Grand Unified Theories With Radiatively Induced Symmetry Breaking | journal = Phys. Rev. Lett. | volume = 48 | issue = 17 | pages = 1220–1223 | doi= 10.1103/PhysRevLett.48.1220 | bibcode = 1982PhRvL..48.1220A}}</ref> (and, independently, [[Andrei Linde]]) constructed the first inflationary models that could speed up the expansion of the [[universe]] enough to explain the observed smoothness and flatness of the universe and then "gracefully exit" to the more modest expansion observed today.<ref>{{cite journal | last1= Albrecht | first1 = A. | last2 = Steinhardt | first2 = P.J.| year =1982 | title = Reheating an Inflationary Universe | journal = Phys. Rev. Lett. | volume = 48 | issue = 20 | pages = 1437–1440 | doi = 10.1103/PhysRevLett.48.1437 | bibcode = 1982PhRvL..48.1437A}}</ref>  The Albrecht-Steinhardt paper was the first to note the effect of Hubble friction in sustaining inflation for a sufficiently long period (the "slow-roll" effect), setting the prototype for most subsequent inflationary models.

Hubble friction played a critical role in the 1983 paper by James Bardeen, Steinhardt and Michael S. Turner<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Bardeen | first1 = J. M. | last2 = Steinhardt | first2 = P. J. | last3 = Turner | first3 = M. S. | year = 1983 | title = Spontaneous Creation Of Almost Scale-Free Density Perturbations In An Inflationary Universe | journal = Phys. Rev. D | volume = 28 | issue = 4 | pages = 679–693 |doi = 10.1103/PhysRevD.28.679 | bibcode = 1983PhRvD..28..679B}}</ref> who were the first to introduce a reliable, relativistically gauge invariant method to compute how quantum fluctuations during inflation might naturally generate a nearly scale-invariant spectrum of density fluctuations with a small tilt, properties later shown by observations of the cosmic microwave background to be features of our universe. The density fluctuations are seeds about which galaxies eventually form. Contemporaneous calculations by several other groups obtained similar conclusions using less rigorous methods.

====Eternal inflation and the multiverse====
In 1982, Steinhardt presented the first example of [[eternal inflation]].<ref name="steinhardt">{{cite book| editor1-last=Gibbons| editor1-first= Gary W.| editor1-link= Gary Gibbons| editor2-first = Stephen W.| editor2-last = Hawking| editor3-last = Siklos| editor3-first= S.T.C. |title= The Very Early Universe |chapter= Natural Inflation|publisher=Cambridge University Press |pages = 251–66| year=1983 |isbn=978-0-521-31677-4}}</ref> Neverending inflation was eventually shown to be a generic feature of inflationary models that leads to a [[multiverse]], the break-up of space into an infinite multitude of patches spanning an infinite range of outcomes instead of the single smooth and flat universe, as originally hoped when first proposed.

Although some cosmologists would later come to embrace the multiverse, Steinhardt consistently expressed his concern that it utterly destroys the predictive power of the theory he helped create.  Because the inflationary theory leads to a multiverse that allows for every possible outcome, Steinhardt argued, we must conclude that the inflationary theory actually predicts nothing.<ref name="Inflation Debate">{{cite journal| author = Steinhardt, Paul J.| title = Inflation Debate: Is the theory at the heart of modern cosmology deeply flawed?| journal = Scientific American|date=April 2011| url = http://www.physics.princeton.edu/~steinh/0411036.pdf|doi = 10.1038/scientificamerican0411-36| pmid = 21495480| volume=304| issue = 4| pages=36–43| bibcode = 2011SciAm.304d..36S}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Steinhardt |first=Paul J. |title=The Cyclic Theory of the Universe |url=https://www.prsinstitute.org/downloads/related/natural-sciences/cosmology/TheCyclicTheoryoftheUniverse.pdf |access-date=4 November 2023 |website=www.prsinstitute.org}}</ref><ref name="physicist-slams-cosmic-theory-he-helped-conceive">{{citation| url= http://blogs.scientificamerican.com/cross-check/physicist-slams-cosmic-theory-he-helped-conceive/ | title= Physicist Slams Cosmic Theory He Helped Conceive | last1=Horgan| last2= John |date= December 1, 2014|work = Scientific American }}</ref>

In 1993, Robert Crittenden, Rick Davis, J.R. Bond, G. Efstathiou and Steinhardt performed the first calculations of the complete imprint of gravitational waves on the [[cosmic microwave background|B-mode]] temperature maps and on the polarization of the microwave background radiation.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Crittenden | first1 = R. | last2 = Bond | first2 = J.R. | last3 = Davis | first3 = R.L. | last4 = Efstathiou | first4 = G.E. | last5 = Steinhardt | first5 = P. J. | year = 1993 | title = The Imprint of Gravitational Waves on the Cosmic Microwave Background | journal = Phys. Rev. Lett. | volume = 71 | issue = 3 | pages = 324–327 | doi = 10.1103/PhysRevLett.71.324 | bibcode = 1993PhRvL..71..324C|arxiv = astro-ph/9303014 | pmid=10055242| s2cid = 18553924 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Crittenden | last2 = Davis | first2 = R.L. | last3 = Steinhardt | first3 = P. J. | year = 1993 | title = Polarization of the Microwave Background due to Primordial Gravitational Waves | journal = Astrophysical Journal Letters | volume = 417 | pages = L13–L16 | doi=10.1086/187082 | bibcode = 1993ApJ...417L..13C|arxiv = astro-ph/9306027 | s2cid = 18194291 }}</ref>

Despite his criticisms of the idea, Steinhardt's major contributions to the inflationary theory were recognized in 2002 when he shared the Dirac Prize with [[Alan Guth]] of [[M.I.T.]] and [[Andrei Linde]] of [[Stanford]].<ref name="Dirac Prize" >{{cite web|url=https://www.ictp.it/|title=ICTP - International Centre for Theoretical Physics|website=www.ictp.it|access-date=28 January 2019}}</ref>

In 2013, Anna Ijjas, [[Avi Loeb|Abraham Loeb]] and Steinhardt added to the criticisms in a widely discussed pair of papers that the inflationary model was much less likely to explain our universe than previously thought.<ref name="2013 Planck 1">{{cite journal | last1 = Iijas | first1 = Anna | last2 = Loeb | first2 = Abraham| last3 = Steinhardt | first3 = Paul | year = 2013 | title = Inflationary Paradigm in trouble after Planck 2013 | journal = Phys. Lett. B | volume = 723 | issue= 4–5 | pages = 261–266 | doi = 10.1016/j.physletb.2013.05.023|arxiv = 1304.2785 |bibcode = 2013PhLB..723..261I | s2cid = 14875751 }}</ref><ref name="2013 Planck 2">{{cite journal | last1 = Iijas  | first1 = Anna | last2 = Steinhardt  | first2 = Paul J. | last3 =Loeb  | first3 = Abraham  | year = 2014 | title = Inflationary Schism | journal = Phys. Lett. B | volume = 7 | pages = 142–146 | doi = 10.1016/j.physletb.2014.07.012 |bibcode = 2014PhLB..736..142I | arxiv = 1402.6980| s2cid = 119096427 }}</ref>

According to their analysis of the Planck satellite 2013 results, the chances of obtaining a universe matching the observations after a period of inflation is less than one in a [[googolplex]].<ref>{{Cite news| url =https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IWy8OGztbnE | title = Filling the Big Gap in Einstein's Theory, Paul Steinhardt TEDxCLESalon | work = YouTube | access-date = September 21, 2016}}</ref> Steinhardt and his team dubbed the result the "unlikeliness problem." The two papers also showed that Planck satellite data ruled out what had been historically accepted as the simplest inflationary models and that the remaining inflationary models require more parameters, more fine-tuning of those parameters, and more unlikely initial conditions.<ref name="2013 Planck 1"/><ref name="2013 Planck 2"/>

In 2015, the unlikeness problem was reaffirmed and strengthened by a subsequent round of measurements reported by the Planck satellite team.

In 2018, Steinhardt, in collaboration with Prateek Agrawal, George Obieds, and [[Cumrun Vafa]], argued that inflation may also be incompatible with string theory because inflationary models generally violate constraints (sometimes called the "swampland conjectures") on what is required for a model to be consistent with [[quantum gravity]].<ref name="Swampland">{{cite journal | last1 = Obied | first1 = Georges | last2 = Ooguri | first2 = Hirosi| last3 = Steinhardt | first3 = Paul J. | year = 2018 | title = On the Cosmological Implications of the String Swampland | journal = Phys. Lett. B | volume = 784| pages = 271–276| doi = 10.1016/j.physletb.2018.07.040|arxiv = 1806.09718 |bibcode = 2018PhLB..784..271A| s2cid = 119252887 }}</ref>

===Bouncing and cyclic cosmology===
Motivated by what he viewed as the failures of inflationary theory, including but not limited to the multiverse, Steinhardt became a leading developer of a new class of cosmological models that replace the so-called big bang with a bounce and replace inflation with a period of slow contraction preceding the bounce. The hypothetical idea that the universe began with a bang is based on extrapolating back in time, assuming that [[Einstein's equations]] of [[general relativity]] remain valid at energies and temperatures far greater than have ever been tested.

Theorists generally agree that, if there was a big bang, then, in the instants following, quantum physics effects should have created large fluctuations in spacetime.   These fluctuations would have caused space-time to curve and warp and the distribution of energy to become very uneven, all of which is inconsistent with what experimentalists observe when they study the early universe. The universe is, in fact, observed to be homogeneous.<ref>{{Cite news| url=https://www.esa.int/Science_Exploration/Space_Science/Planck/Planck_reveals_an_almost_perfect_Universe  | title = Planck reveals an almost perfect Universe | work = ESA | access-date = January 21, 2024}}</ref> Inflation was originally invented to explain the smoothness that is observed in the universe. But it is unclear how to transition from the highly uneven conditions created after a big bang to an inflationary universe and, even if a solution could be found, the inflationary theory ultimately results in  a multiverse rather than a smooth universe.<ref name="physicist-slams-cosmic-theory-he-helped-conceive"/>

The new approach removes the bang altogether, envisioning instead a smooth transition from a previous period of slow contraction to the current period of expansion. If the contraction is slow, it smooths the entire universe, and, unlike inflation there is no multiverse. By evading the infamous cosmic singularity problem associated with a big bang,  a bounce avoids quantum gravity effects that produce an unsmooth universe. A natural extension of these ideas is a never-beginning and never-ending cyclic universe in which epochs of bounce, expansion, and contraction repeat at regular intervals.

In a pivotal lecture in 2021, Steinhardt explained why it is time to jettison the big bang theory and replace the bang with a 'bounce' — a smooth transition from contraction to a dense, hot universe that continues to expand and cool. 
<ref>{{Cite news| url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=S7-HNi2ne44 | title = Paul Steinhardt – Time to Take the 'Big Bang' out of the Big Bang Theory?| work = YouTube | access-date = January 21, 2024}}</ref>

====Historical development====
=====Early models with a big crunch=====
In 2001, Steinhardt presented the first examples of these bouncing and cyclic models, referred to as "ekpyrotic," in papers with Justin Khoury, Burt A. Ovrut and Neil Turok.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Khoury | first1 = J. | last2 = Ovrut | first2 = B.| last3 = Steinhardt | first3 = P. J. | year = 2001 | title = The Ekpyrotic Universe: Colliding Branes and the Origin of the Hot Big Bang | journal = Phys. Rev. D | volume = 64 | issue=12 | article-number = 123522 | doi = 10.1103/PhysRevD.64.123522 |arxiv = hep-th/0103239 |bibcode = 2001PhRvD..64l3522K | s2cid = 374628 }}</ref>

These models were based on the speculative notion suggested by string theory that the universe has extra-dimensions bounded by "branes" (where "brane" is derived from "membrane," a basic object in string theory).  The fiery collision and rebound of these branes is comparable to a big crunch, a violent event that would depend sensitively on strong quantum gravity effects that are not yet established and may create tremendous curvature and warping of spacetime.

In principle, the collisions can repeat at regular intervals resulting in a cyclic universe.<ref name="physicist-slams-cosmic-theory-he-helped-conceive"/> In 2002, Steinhardt and Turok incorporated the ekpyrotic idea into an early version of a cyclic theory of the universe.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Steinhardt | first1 = P. J. | last2=Turok | first2=N.| title = A Cyclic Model of the Universe | journal = [[Science (journal)|Science]] | volume = 296 | issue = 5572 | pages = 1436–1439 | date = 2002-04-25 | doi = 10.1126/science.1070462 | bibcode = 2002Sci...296.1436S | arxiv = hep-th/0111030 | pmid=11976408| s2cid = 1346107 }}</ref>

=====Improved models with slow contraction and a gentle bounce=====
Recent versions of bouncing cosmology developed by Anna Ijjas and Steinhardt introduce elements that simplify and address problems with the earlier ekpyrotic proposal.  They do not require extra dimensions or branes or string theory; ordinary fields with potential energy evolving in space-time, similar to inflationary models, can be used.<ref name="New Cyclic">{{cite journal | last1 = Ijjas | first1 = Anna | last2 = Steinhardt | first2 = Paul J.| year = 2019 | title = A new kind of cyclic universe | journal = Phys. Lett. B | volume = 795| pages =666–672 | doi = 10.1016/j.physletb.2019.06.056 |arxiv =1904.08022|bibcode = 2019PhLB..795..666I| s2cid = 118712442 }}</ref>

Instead of a violent ekpyrosis (the collision of two branes), the smoothing and flattening of spacetime occurs through "slow contraction," a period in which space contracts very little while the Hubble radius contracts a lot. By the time the bounce is reached, the universe is "supersmoothed."<ref name="Supersmoothing">{{cite journal | last1 = Cook | first1 = William G. | last2 = Glushchenko | first2 = Iryna A. | last3 = Ijjas | first3 = Anna  | last4 =Pretorius  | first4 =Franz |last5 = Steinhardt | first5 = Paul J.|year = 2020 | title = Supersmoothing through Slow Contraction | journal = Phys. Lett. B | volume = 808| article-number = 135690 | doi = 10.1016/j.physletb.2020.135690 |arxiv = 2006.01172|bibcode = 2020PhLB..80835690C}}</ref>

The bounce is a gentle transition that can be fully computed and maintains smoothness because it is a continuous process that occurs long before quantum gravity effects become strong.  There is no cosmic singularity problem, unlike theories based on the big bang.

=====Universal smoothing and ultralocality=====
To test these ideas, Anna Ijjas adapted the tools of numerical general relativity, originally invented to simulate the merger of black holes and the emission of gravitational waves, to cosmology. Together with Steinhardt and collaborators, the new tools were used to study the effectiveness of slow contraction.<ref name="Supersmoothing"/><ref>{{cite journal |last1 = Ijjas| first1 = Anna | last2 = Cook | first2 = William G.| last3 = Pretorius | first3 = Franz  | last4 = Steinhardt | first4 = Paul J.|last5 = Davies | first5 = Elliot Y.|year = 2020 | title = Robustness of slow contraction to cosmic initial conditions   | journal = JCAP | volume = 2020 | issue = 8 | page = 030 | doi = 10.1088/1475-7516/2020/08/030 |arxiv = 2006.04999v2 |bibcode = 2020JCAP...08..030I}}</ref><ref name="Initial conditions">{{cite journal | last1 = Garfinkle | first1 = David | last2 = Ijjas | first2 = Anna | last3 = Steinhardt | first3 = Paul J.|year = 2023 | title = Initial conditions problem in cosmological inflation revisited | journal = Phys. Lett. B | volume = 843| article-number = 138028 | doi = 10.1016/j.physletb.2023.138028 |arxiv = 2304.12150|bibcode = 2023PhLB..84338028G}}</ref>

The study demonstrates that slow contraction is a supersmoothing cosmological phase that homogenizes, isotropizes and flattens the universe both classically and quantum mechanically and can do so far more robustly and rapidly than had been realized in earlier studies.
 
Beginning from wildly unsmooth and curvy starting condition, the studies verified that slow contraction smooths virtually all of spacetime due to an effect of general relativity known as ultralocality.<ref name="Ultralocality">{{cite journal | last1 = Ijjas| first1 = Anna | last2 = Sullivan | first2= Andrew P. | last3 = Pretorius | first3 = Frans | last4 = Steinhardt | first4 = Paul J.|last5 =Cook | first5 = William G.|year = 2021 | title = Ultralocality and Slow Contraction | journal = JCAP | volume = 2021| issue = 6 | page = 013 | doi =10.1088/1475-7516/2021/06/013 |arxiv = 2103.00584v1 |bibcode = 2021JCAP...06..013I}}</ref> The ultralocal effect is specific to a contracting universe, and there is no equivalent in an expanding universe, including the case of inflation. The consequent smoothing power is an unparalleled advantage of slow contraction.

=====Cyclic version of bouncing cosmology=====
In the cyclic version of these models, space never crunches; rather, it necessarily grows by a constant factor overall from bounce to bounce every 100 billion years or so. After each bounce, gravitational energy is converted into the matter and radiation that fuels the next cycle. To an observer, the evolution appears to be cyclic because the temperature, density, number of stars and galaxies, etc., are on average the same from one cyclic to the next and the observer cannot see far enough to know that there is an ever-increasing amount of space, matter energy outside the horizon. The fact that the universe expands overall from cycle to cycle means that the entropy produced in earlier cycles (by the formation of stars and other entropy-producing processes) is increasingly diluted as the cycles proceed and so does not have any physical effect on cosmic evolution.<ref name="New Cyclic"/> This growth from cycle to cycle and associated entropy dilution are features that distinguish these new cyclic models from versions discussed in the 1920s by Friedmann and Tolman, and explain how the new cyclic model avoids the "entropy problem" that beset earlier versions.

====Theoretical advantages of the new cyclic model====
The new cyclic models have two important advantages over [[inflation (physics)|inflation]]ary models. First, because they do not include inflation, they do not produce a multiverse. As a result, unlike inflation, cyclic models produce a single universe that everywhere have the same predicted properties that are subject to empirical tests.  Second, cyclic models explain why there must be dark energy. According to these models, the accelerated expansion caused by dark energy starts the smoothing process, the decay of dark energy to other forms of energy starts a period of slow contraction, and the slow contraction is what is responsible for smoothing and flattening the universe.<ref name="New Cyclic"/>

====Theoretical predictions of the new cyclic model====
One prediction of the cyclic models is that, unlike inflation, no detectable gravitational waves are generated during the smoothing and flattening process. The Simons Observatory being built in the Atacama Desert in Chile will test this prediction.  Instead, the prediction of the cyclic models is that the only source of gravitational waves on cosmic wavelength scales are so-called "secondary gravitational waves" that are produced long after the bounce. Their amplitudes are far too weak to be found in current detectors but are ultimately detectable.  A second prediction is that the current acceleration expansion must eventually stop and the vacuum must be eventually decay in order to initiate the next cycle.<ref name="New Cyclic"/>(Other predictions depend on the specific fields (or branes) that cause the contraction.)

====Observational support for the new cyclic model====
The cyclic model may naturally explain why the [[cosmological constant]] is exponentially small and positive, compared to the enormous value expected by [[quantum (physics)|quantum]] gravity theories.<ref name="Cosmo constant">{{cite journal | last1 = Steinhardt | first1 = P. J. | last2=Turok | first2=N.| title = Why the cosmological constant is small and positive | journal = [[Science (journal)|Science]] | volume = 312 | issue = 5777 | pages = 1180–1182| doi = 10.1126/science.1126231 | bibcode = 2006Sci...312.1180S| arxiv =astro-ph/0605173 | pmid=16675662| year = 2006 | s2cid = 14178620 }}</ref>  The cosmological constant might begin large, as expected, but then might slowly decay over the course of many cycles to the tiny value observed today.

The discovery of the [[Higgs field]] at the [[Large Hadron Collider]] (LHC) may provide added support for the cyclic model.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Bars | first1 = I. | last2 = Steinhardt | first2 = P.J.| last3 = Turok | first3 = N | year = 2013 | title = Cyclic cosmology, conformal symmetry and the metastability of the Higgs | journal = Phys. Lett. B | volume = 726 | issue=1–3 | pages = 50–55 |doi=10.1016/j.physletb.2013.08.071|arxiv = 1307.8106 |bibcode = 2013PhLB..726...50B | s2cid = 592287 }}</ref>  Evidence from the LHC suggests that the current vacuum may decay in the future, according to calculations made by Steinhardt, Turok and Itzhak Bars. The decay of the current vacuum is required by the cyclic model in order to end the current phase of expansion, contract, bounce and begin a new era of expansion; the Higgs provides a possible mechanism of decay that can be tested. The Higgs field is a viable candidate for the field that drives the cycles of expansion and contraction, and this may ultimately be testable.

===Dark energy and dark matter===
Steinhardt has made significant contributions researching the "dark side" of the universe: [[dark energy]], the [[cosmological constant]] problem and [[dark matter]].

In 1995, Steinhardt and [[Jeremiah Ostriker]] used a concordance of cosmological observations to show there must be a non-zero dark energy component today, more than 65 percent of the total energy density, sufficient to cause the expansion of the universe to accelerate.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Ostriker | first1 = J. P. | last2=Steinhardt | first2= P.J.| title = The observational case for a low-density Universe with a non-zero cosmological constant | journal = [[Nature (journal)|Nature]] | volume = 377 | issue = 6550| pages = 600–602 | date = 1995| doi = 10.1038/377600a0 | bibcode = 1995Natur.377..600O| s2cid = 4236645 }}</ref> This was verified three years later by supernova observations in 1998.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Riess | first1 = A. | last2 = al. | first2 = et | year = 1998 | title = Observational Evidence from Supernovae for an Accelerating Universe and a Cosmological Constant | journal = [[The Astronomical Journal]] | volume = 116 | issue = 3 | pages = 1009–1038| doi= 10.1086/300499 | bibcode = 1998AJ....116.1009R|arxiv = astro-ph/9805201 | s2cid = 15640044 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Perlmutter | first1 = S. | author1-link =Saul Perlmutter| last2 = al. | first2 = et | year = 1999 | title = Measurements of Omega and Lamba from 42 High-Redshift Supernovae | journal = The Astrophysical Journal | volume = 517 | issue = 2 | pages = 565–586| doi= 10.1086/307221 | bibcode = 1999ApJ...517..565P|arxiv = astro-ph/9812133 | s2cid = 118910636 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Bahcall | first1 = N.A. | author1-link =Neta Bahcall| last2 = Ostriker | first2 = J.P.| author2-link =Jeremiah P. Ostriker | last3 = Perlmutter | first3 = S. | last4 = Steinhardt | first4 = P.J. | year = 1999 | title = The Cosmic Triangle: Revealing the State of the Universe | journal = [[Science (journal)|Science]] | volume = 284 | issue = 5419| pages = 1481–1488 | doi= 10.1126/science.284.5419.1481 | bibcode = 1999Sci...284.1481B|arxiv = astro-ph/9906463 | s2cid = 15271568 }}</ref>

Working with colleagues, he subsequently introduced the concept of [[quintessence (physics)|quintessence]], a form of dark energy that varies with time.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Caldwell | first1 = R.R. | last2 = Dave | first2 = R.| last3 = Steinhardt | first3 = P.J. | year = 1998 | title = Cosmological Imprint of an Energy Component with General Equation-of-State | journal = [[Phys. Rev. Lett.]] | volume = 80 | issue = 8 | pages = 1582–1585 | doi = 10.1103/PhysRevLett.80.1582 | bibcode = 1998PhRvL..80.1582C|arxiv = astro-ph/9708069 | s2cid = 597168 | url = https://cds.cern.ch/record/331639 }}</ref> It was first posited by Steinhardt's team as an alternative to the cosmological constant, which is (by definition) constant and static; quintessence is dynamic.  Its energy density and pressure evolve over time. The 2018 paper on swampland conjectures with Agrawal, Obieds and Vafa<ref name="Swampland"/> points to quintessence as being the only option for dark energy in string theory and consistent quantum gravity.

In 2000, [[David Spergel]] and Steinhardt first introduced the concept of strongly [[self-interacting dark matter]] (SIDM) to explain various anomalies in standard cold dark models based on assuming dark matter consists of [[weakly interacting massive particles]] (also referred to as "WIMPs").<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Spergel | first1 = D.N. | last2 = Steinhardt | first2 = P.J. | year = 2000 | title = Observational Evidence for Self-Interacting Cold Dark Matter | journal = Phys. Rev. Lett. | volume = 84 | issue = 17 | pages = 3760–3763 | doi = 10.1103/PhysRevLett.84.3760 | bibcode = 2000PhRvL..84.3760S|arxiv = astro-ph/9909386 | pmid=11019199| s2cid = 6669358 | url = https://cds.cern.ch/record/401299 }}</ref>

In 2014, Steinhardt, Spergel and Jason Pollack have proposed that a small fraction of dark matter could have ultra-strong self-interactions, which would cause the particles to coalesce rapidly and collapse into seeds for early [[supermassive black holes]].<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Pollack | first1 = Jason | last2 = Spergel | first2 = David N. | author2-link =David Spergel| last3= Steinhardt | first3 = Paul J. | year = 2014 | title = Supermassive Black Holes from Ultra-Strongly Self-Interacting Dark Matter | arxiv = 1501.00017 | journal = The Astrophysical Journal| volume = 804 | issue = 2 | page = 131| doi =10.1088/0004-637X/804/2/131 | bibcode = 2015ApJ...804..131P| s2cid = 15916893 }}</ref>

===Quasicrystals===
====Development of the theory====
In 1983, Steinhardt and his then-student Dov Levine first introduced the theoretical concept of [[quasicrystal]]s in a patent disclosure.<ref name="The Second Kind of Impossible" /> The complete theory was published the following year in a paper entitled "Quasicrystals: A New Class of Ordered Structures."<ref name="Quasicrystals" >{{cite journal | last1 = Levine | first1 = D. | last2 = Steinhardt | first2 = P.J. | year = 1984 | title = Quasicrystals: A New Class of Ordered Structures | url = http://physics.princeton.edu/~steinh/LevineSteinhardt1.pdf | journal = Phys. Rev. Lett. | volume = 53 | issue = 26 | pages = 2477–2480 | doi = 10.1103/PhysRevLett.53.2477 | bibcode = 1984PhRvL..53.2477L| doi-access = free }}</ref> The theory proposed the existence of a new phase of solid matter analogous to Penrose tilings with rotational symmetries previously thought to be impossible for solids. Steinhardt and Levine named the new phase of matter a "quasicrystal." The never-before-seen [[atomic structure]] had quasiperiodic atomic ordering, rather than the periodic ordering characteristic of conventional [[crystal]]s.

The new theory overturned 200 years of scientific dogma and proved that quasicrystals could violate all of the previously accepted mathematical theorems about the symmetry of matter. Symmetries once thought to be forbidden for solids are actually possible for quasicrystals, including solids with axes of five-fold symmetry and three-dimensional [[icosahedral]] symmetry.

====The first reported example of a synthetic quasicrystal====
Working simultaneously to, but independently of, Steinhardt and Levine, [[Dan Shechtman]], Ilan Blech, Denis Gratias and [[John Cahn]] at the [[National Bureau of Standards]] (NBS) were focused on an experimental discovery they could not explain. It was an unusual [[alloy]] of manganese and aluminum with a [[diffraction pattern]] of what appeared to be sharp (though not perfectly point-like) spots arranged with icosahedral symmetry that did not fit any known crystal structure.<ref name=NBS>{{cite journal | last1 = Shechtman | first1 = D. | last2 = Blech | first2 = I.| last3 = Gratias | first3 = D. | last4 = Cahn | first4 = J.W. | year = 1984 | title = Metallic Phase with Long-Range Orientational Order and No Translational Symmetry | journal = Phys. Rev. Lett. | volume = 53 | issue = 20 | pages = 1951–1953 | doi = 10.1103/PhysRevLett.53.1951 | bibcode = 1984PhRvL..53.1951S| doi-access = free }}</ref> The alloy was first noted in 1982, but results were not published until November 1984 after more convincing data had been obtained.<ref name="The Second Kind of Impossible"/>

Steinhardt and Levine were shown a preprint of the Shechtman team's paper and immediately recognized that it could be experimental proof of their still-unpublished quasicrystal theory.<ref name="The Second Kind of Impossible"/> The theory, along with the proposal that it could explain the mysterious, forbidden structure of the new alloy was published in December 1984.<ref name="Quasicrystals"/>

The new alloy was ultimately discovered to be problematic. It proved to be unstable and the noted imperfections in the diffraction pattern allowed for multiple explanations (including one about [[crystal twinning]] proposed by [[Linus Pauling]]) that were hotly debated for the next few years.<ref name="The Second Kind of Impossible" />

In 1987, An-Pang Tsai and his group at Japan's [[Tohoku University]] made an important breakthrough with the [[Chemical synthesis|synthesis]] of the first-ever stable [[icosahedral]] quasicrystal. It had sharp diffraction spots arranged in close accord with Steinhardt and Levine's quasicrystal theory and was inconsistent with any of the alternative explanations.<ref name="iopscience.iop.org">{{cite journal | last1 = Tsai | first1 = An-Pang | last2 = Inoue | first2 = Akihisa | last3 = Masumoto | first3 = Tsuyoshi | year = 1987 | title = A Stable Quasicrystal in Al-Cu-Fe System | journal = Japanese Journal of Applied Physics | volume = 26 | issue = Part 2, Number 9 | pages = L1505–L1507| doi = 10.1143/JJAP.26.L1505|bibcode = 1987JaJAP..26L1505T | s2cid = 98442801 }}</ref> The theoretical debate was effectively ended and the Steinhardt-Levine theory gained wide acceptance.<ref name="The Second Kind of Impossible"/>

[[File:Khatyrkite sample.png|thumb|right|Small sample, about 3 mm across, of a [[Khatyrkite]]-bearing [[meteorite]] (top and bottom left panels)from the mineral collection at the Museo di Storia Naturale in Florence, Italy. On January 2, 2009, Paul Steinhardt and Nan Yao identified the first known natural quasicrystal embedded in the sample (area of discovery indicated by red circle in bottom right panel).]]

====The first natural quasicrystal====
In 1999, Steinhardt assembled a team at [[Princeton University]] to search for a natural quasicrystal. The team, composed of Peter Lu, Ken Deffeyes and Nan Yao, devised a novel mathematical algorithm to search through an international database of powder diffraction patterns.<ref name="The Second Kind of Impossible" /><ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Lu | first1 = P. | last2 = Deffreyes | first2 = K.| last3 = Steinhardt | first3 = P.J.  | last4 = Yao | year = 2001 | title = Identifying and Indexing Icosahedral Quasicrystals from Powder Diffraction Patterns | journal = Phys. Rev. Lett. | volume = 87  | issue = 27 | article-number = 275507 | doi = 10.1103/PhysRevLett.87.275507 | pmid=11800896|arxiv = cond-mat/0108259 |bibcode = 2001PhRvL..87A5507L | s2cid = 2814118 }}</ref>

For the first eight years, the search yielded no results. In 2007, Italian scientist [[Luca Bindi]], then curator of the mineral collection at the Universite' di Firenze, joined the team.<ref name="The Second Kind of Impossible"/> Two years later, Bindi identified a promising specimen in his museum's storage room.<ref name="Natural Quasicrystals">{{cite journal | last1 = Bindi| first1 = L. | last2= Steinhardt | first2= P.J.| last3= Yao | first3 = N.| last4 = Lu | first4 = P.| title = Natural Quasicrystals | journal = [[Science (journal)|Science]] | volume = 324 | issue = 5932 | pages = 1306–1309 | date = 2009 | doi = 10.1126/science.1170827 | bibcode = 2009Sci...324.1306B| pmid=19498165| s2cid = 14512017 }}</ref> The tiny specimen, a few millimeters across, had been packed away in a box labeled "[[khatyrkite]]," which is an ordinary crystal composed of copper and aluminum. On January 2, 2009, Steinhardt and Nan Yao, director of the Princeton Imaging Center, examined the material and identified the signature diffraction pattern of an icosahedral quasicrystal. This was the first known natural [[quasicrystal]].<ref name="Natural Quasicrystals"/>

[[File:Icosahedrite Diffraction Pattern.jpg|thumb|The electron diffraction pattern for [[icosahedrite]], the first natural quasicrystal, obtained by aiming the electron beam down a fivefold axis of symmetry. The patterns correspond perfectly (up to experimental resolution) with the fivefold patterns first predicted by Paul Steinhardt and Dov Levine in the 1980s for an icosahedral quasicrystal.]]
The [[International Mineralogical Association]] accepted the quasicrystal as a new [[mineral]] and designated its name, [[icosahedrite]].<ref name="Natural Quasicrystals"/> The material had exactly the same atomic composition (Al<sub>63</sub>Cu<sub>24</sub>Fe<sub>13</sub>) as the first [[thermodynamic]]ally stable quasicrystal synthesized by An-Pang Tsai and his group in their laboratory in 1987.

====Expedition to Chukotka====
Two years after identifying the museum sample, Steinhardt organized an international team of experts and led them on an expedition to its source, the remote [[Iomrautvaam|Listventovyi stream]] in the [[Chukotka Autonomous Okrug]] in the northern half of the [[Kamchatka Peninsula]] in far eastern Russia.   The team included Bindi and Valery Kryachko, the Russian ore geologist who had found the original samples of khatyrkite crystal while working at the Listventovyi stream in 1979.<ref name="The Second Kind of Impossible"/> [[File:Bindi, Kryachko, Steinhardt.JPG|thumb|right| On location at the Listventovyi stream in the Kamchatka Peninsula in 2011 (left to right): [[Luca Bindi]] (University of Firenze, Italy), Valery Kryachko (IGEM, Russia) and Paul Steinhardt (Princeton, US)]] Other members of the team were: Chris Andronicos, Vadim Distler, Michael Eddy, Alexander Kostin, Glenn MacPherson, Marina Yudovskaya, and Steinhardt's son, William Steinhardt.<ref name="The Second Kind of Impossible"/>

After digging and panning a ton and a half of clay along the banks of the Listvenitovyi stream in the [[Koryak Mountains]], eight different grains containing icosahedrite were identified.<ref name="The Second Kind of Impossible"/>  During subsequent years of study, Steinhardt's team proved that both the sample found in the Florence museum and the samples recovered from the field in Chukotka originated from a meteorite formed 4.5 billion years ago (before there were planets), and landed on the Earth about 15,000 years ago.<ref>{{cite journal| last1 = Wolchover | first1= Natalie|title= In a grain, a Glimpse of the Cosmos|journal =[[Quanta Magazine]]| date= 13 June 2014|url=https://www.quantamagazine.org/20140613-quasicrystal-meteorite-poses-age-old-questions/| access-date= October 11, 2015}}</ref>

====More natural quasicrystals====
Further studies revealed other new minerals in the Chukotka samples.  In 2014, one of those minerals was discovered to be a crystalline phase of aluminum, nickel and iron ({{chem2|Al38Ni33Fe30}}). It was accepted by the International Mineralogical Association and named "steinhardtite" in Steinhardt's honor<ref name="steinhardtite">{{cite web | url=http://wwwphy.princeton.edu/~steinh/STEINHARDTITE%20LETTER.pdf | title=Letter to Luca Bindi | publisher=School of Science and Health, [[Western Sydney University]] / Paul J. Steinhardt | date=July 1, 2014 | access-date=January 29, 2019 | author=Williams, Professor Peter | archive-date=April 7, 2022 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220407131139/http://wwwphy.princeton.edu/~steinh/STEINHARDTITE%20LETTER.pdf }}</ref> In 2015, a second type of natural quasicrystal was discovered in a different grain of the same meteorite. The second known natural quasicrystal was found to be a different mixture of aluminum, nickel and iron ({{chem2|Al71Ni24Fe5}}) and had a decagonal symmetry (a regularly stacking of atomic layers which each have 10-fold symmetry). It was accepted by the International Mineralogical Association and given the name "decagonite."<ref name="nature.com">{{cite journal | last1 = Bindi | first1 = Luca | last2= Yao | first2= Nan | last3 = Lin | first3 = Chaney | last4 = Hollister | first4 = Lincoln S. | last5 = Andronicos | first5 = Christopher L. | last6 = Distler | first6 = Vadim V. | last7 = Eddy | first7 = Michael P. | last8 = Kostin | first8 = Alexander | last9 = Kryachko | first9 = Valery | last10 = MacPherson | first10 = Glenn J. | last11 = Steinhardt | first11 = William M. | last12 = Yudovskaya | first12 = Marina | last13 = Steinhardt| first13 = Paul J. | title = Natural quasicrystal with decagonal symmetry | journal = [[Nature (journal)|Scientific Reports]] | volume = 5| article-number = 9111| date = 2015 | doi = 10.1038/srep09111 | doi-access = free| bibcode = 2015NatSR...5.9111B| pmid=25765857 | pmc=4357871}}</ref><ref name="mindat.org">{{cite journal|title = Decagonite, Al71Ni24Fe5, a quasicrystal with decagonal symmetry| url = http://www.mindat.org/forum.php?read,14,355062,355062| journal=American Mineralogist |volume=100 |issue=10 |date=October 2015 |doi=10.2138/am-2015-5423 | s2cid = 101528286|url-access=subscription |doi-access=free }}</ref>

Three more crystalline minerals were also discovered and named after colleagues involved in Steinhardt's quasicrystal research: "hollisterite," for Princeton petrologist Lincoln Hollister; "kryachkoite," for Russian geologist Valery Kryachko; and "stolperite," for Caltech's former provost Ed Stolper.<ref name="The Second Kind of Impossible"/>
[[File:Darb-i Imam shrine spandrel.JPG|thumb|right|Girih tile quasicrystal pattern on right half of [[spandrel]] at [[Darb-e Imam]] Shrine ]]

====A previously unknown quasicrystal created by the first atomic bomb test====
In 2021, Steinhardt led the team that discovered a novel icosahedral quasicrystal created by the detonation of the first nuclear device at [[Alamogordo, New Mexico]], on July 16, 1945 (the [[Trinity (nuclear test)|Trinity]] test). The new quasicrystal was discovered within a sample of red [[trinitite]] and is the oldest extant anthropogenic quasicrystal ever discovered.<ref name="Atomic"/> The previously unknown structure, which is made of iron, silicon, copper and calcium, is thought to have been formed by the fusion of vaporized desert sand and copper cables during the atomic test blast.<ref>{{cite journal| last1 = Castelvecchi | first1= Davide |title= First nuclear detonation created 'impossible' quasicrystals |journal =[[Nature (journal)|Nature]]| year= 2021 | volume= 593 | issue= 7860 | page= 487 | doi= 10.1038/d41586-021-01332-0 | pmid= 34007024 | bibcode = 2021Natur.593..487C | s2cid= 234779438 | doi-access= free }}</ref> The discovery of a unique quasicrystal in trinitite could transform the field of [[nuclear forensics]], leading to a new diagnostic tool<ref>{{cite journal| last1 = D'Agostino | first1= Susan|author-link=Susan D'Agostino |title= What are atomic bomb quasicrystals, and why do they matter?|journal =[[Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists]]| date= 9 June 2021 |url= https://thebulletin.org/2021/06/what-are-atomic-bomb-quasicrystals-and-why-do-they-matter/ | access-date= June 13, 2021}}</ref> which could help law enforcement prevent future terrorist attacks by using quasicrystals (which unlike radioactive debris and gases do not decay) to identify the signature of an atomic weapon and track down the culprits.<ref>{{cite journal| last1 = Sloan | first1= Marisa|title= The First Atomic Bomb Created This 'Forbidden' Quasicrystal|journal =[[Discover Magazine]]|url=https://www.discovermagazine.com/the-sciences/the-first-atomic-bomb-created-this-forbidden-quasicrystal/| access-date= July 25, 2021}}</ref>

====Other contributions to the field====
Steinhardt and his collaborators have made significant contributions to understanding the quasicrystals' unique mathematical and physical properties,<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Socolar | first1 = J. | last2 = Steinhardt | first2 = P.J. | year = 1986 | title =Quasicrystals II: Unit Cell Configurations  | url = http://www.physics.princeton.edu/~steinh/QuasiPartII.pdf | journal = Phys. Rev. B | volume = 34  | issue = 2 | pages = 617–647 | doi = 10.1103/PhysRevB.34.617| pmid = 9939668 |bibcode = 1986PhRvB..34..617S }}</ref> including theories of how and why quasicrystals form<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Jeong | first1 = H.C. | last2=Steinhardt | first2= P.J.| title = A simpler approach to Penrose tiling with implications for quasicrystal formation | journal = [[Nature (journal)|Nature]] | volume = 382 | issue = 6590| pages = 431–433 | date = 1996 | doi = 10.1038/382431a0 | bibcode = 1996Natur.382..431S| s2cid = 4354819 }}</ref> and their elastic and [[hydrodynamic]]s properties.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Levine | first1 = D. | last2 = Lubensky | first2 = T.| last3 = Ostlund | first3 = S.  | last4 = Ramaswamy | first4 = S. |  last5 = Steinhardt | first5 = P.J. |  last6=  Toner | first6 = J. | year = 1985 | title = Elasticity and Dislocations in Pentagonal and Icosahedral Quasicrystals | journal = Phys. Rev. Lett. | volume = 54  | issue = 14 | pages = 1520–1523 | doi = 10.1103/PhysRevLett.54.1520 | bibcode = 1985PhRvL..54.1520L | pmid=10031060}}</ref>

[[Peter J. Lu]] and Steinhardt discovered a quasicrystalline [[Islamic]] tiling on the [[Darb-e Imam]] Shrine (1453 A.D.) in [[Isfahan]], Iran constructed from [[girih tiles]].<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Lu | first1 = P. | last2= Steinhardt | first2= P.J.| title = Decagonal and Quasicrystalline Tilings in Medieval Islamic Architecture | journal = [[Science (journal)|Science]] | volume = 315 | issue = 5815 | pages = 1106–1110 | date = 2007 | doi = 10.1126/science.1135491 | bibcode = 2007Sci...315.1106L| pmid=17322056| s2cid = 10374218 }}</ref> In 2007, they deciphered the manner in which early artists created increasingly complex periodic [[girih]] patterns. Those early designs were shown to have culminated in the development of a nearly perfect quasi-[[crystalline]] pattern five centuries before the discovery of Penrose patterns and the Steinhardt-Levine quasicrystal theory.<ref name="The Second Kind of Impossible"/>

===Photonics and hyperuniformity===
Steinhardt's research on [[quasicrystal]]s and other non-[[crystalline solids]] expanded into work on designer materials with novel [[photonic]] and phononic properties.

'''Photonic quasicrystals'''

A team of researchers including Steinhardt, Paul Chaikin, Weining Man and Mischa Megens designed and tested the first photonic quasicrystal with [[icosahedral symmetry]] in 2005. They were the first to demonstrate the existence of photonic band gaps ("PBGs").<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Man | first1 = W. | last2= Megens | first2= M.| last3= Steinhardt | first3 = P.J. | last4 = Chaikin | first4 = P. | title = Experimental Measurement of the Photonic Properties of Icosahedral Quasicrystals  | journal = [[Nature (journal)|Nature]] | volume = 436 | issue = 7053| pages = 993–996 | date = 2005 | doi = 10.1038/nature03977 | bibcode = 2005Natur.436..993M| pmid=16107842| s2cid = 4408304 }}</ref> These materials block light for a finite range of frequencies (or colors) and let pass light with frequencies outside that band, similar to the way in which a [[semiconductor]] blocks electrons for a finite range of energies.

'''Hyperuniform disordered solids (HUDS)'''

Working with [[Salvatore Torquato]] and Marian Florescu, in 2009 Steinhardt discovered a new class of photonic materials called [[Disordered hyperuniformity|hyperuniform disordered solids]] (HUDS), and showed that solids consisting of a hyperuniform disordered arrangement of dielectric elements produce band gaps with perfect spherical symmetry.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Florescu | first1 = M. | last2= Torquato | first2= S.| last3= Steinhardt | first3 = Paul J.  | title = Designer disordered materials with large, complete photonic band gaps | journal = Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences | volume = 106 | issue = 49 | pages = 20658–20663| date = 2009 | doi = 10.1073/pnas.0907744106 | bibcode = 2009PNAS..10620658F| arxiv = 1007.3554| pmid=19918087 | pmc=2777962 | doi-access = free }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Man | first1 = W. | last2= al. | first2= et | title = Isotropic band gaps and freeform waveguides observed in hyperuniform disordered photonic solids | journal = Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences  | volume = 110 | issue = 40 | pages = 15886–15891  | date = 2013 | doi = 10.1073/pnas.1307879110 | bibcode = 2013PNAS..11015886M| arxiv = 1311.2632| pmid=24043795 | pmc=3791749| doi-access = free }}</ref> These materials, which act as isotropic semiconductors for light, can be used to control and manipulate light in a wide range of applications including [[optical communications]], photonic computers, energy harvesting, [[non-linear optics]] and improved light sources.

'''Phoamtonics'''

In 2019, Steinhardt, along with Michael Klatt and Torquato, introduced the idea of "phoamtonics," which refers to photonic materials based on foam-like designs.<ref>{{cite journal | last1=Klatt | first1 = Michael A. |last2 = Torquato | first2 = Salvatore | last3= Steinhardt | first3 = Paul J.  | title = Phoamtonic designs yield sizeable 3D photonic band gaps | journal = Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences | volume = 116| issue = 47| pages = 23480–23486| date = 2019 | doi = 10.1073/pnas.1912730116 | bibcode = 2019PNAS..11623480K| pmid= 31694882| pmc= 6876150| doi-access = free }}</ref> They showed that large photonic bandgaps could arise in network structures created by converting the foam edges (intersections between foam bubbles) to a dielectric material for the two most famous crystalline foam structures, Kelvin foams and Weiare-Phelan foams.

'''Etaphase Inc.'''

The meta-material breakthroughs by Steinhardt and his Princeton colleagues have valuable commercial applications. In 2012, the scientists helped create a start-up company called Etaphase, which will apply their discoveries to a wide range of high performance products. The inventions will be used in integrated circuits, structural materials, photonics, communications, chip-to-chip communications, intra-chip communications, sensors, datacomm, networking, and solar applications.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://etaphase.com/|title=Etaphase Incorporated|website=Etaphase Incorporated|access-date=28 January 2019}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Advancing photonic functionalities |url=https://torquato.princeton.edu/wp-content/uploads/2021/10/AdvancingPhotonicFunctionalities.pdf |access-date=4 November 2023 |website=torquato.princeton.edu}}</ref>

===Amorphous solids===
Steinhardt's research in disordered forms of matter has centered on the structure and properties of [[glass]]es and [[amorphous semiconductors]], and [[amorphous metals]].

He constructed the first computer generated continuous random network (CRN) model of [[glass]] and [[amorphous silicon]] in 1973, while still an undergraduate at [[Caltech]]. CRNs remain the leading model of amorphous silicon and other [[semiconductors]] today.  Working with Richard Alben and D. Weaire, he used the computer model to predict structural and electronic properties.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Steinhardt | first1 = P. J. | last2 = Alben | first2 = R. | last3 = Duffy | first3 = M. G. | last4 = Polk | first4 = D. E. | year = 1973 | title = Relaxed Continuous Random Network Models  | journal = Phys. Rev. B | volume = 8 | issue = 12 | pages = 6021–6023 | doi = 10.1103/physrevb.8.6021|bibcode = 1973PhRvB...8.6021S }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Alben | first1 = R. | last2 = Weaire | first2 = D. | last3 = Steinhardt | first3 = P.J. | year = 1973 | title = One Band Density of States for the Polk Model  | journal = Journal of Physics | volume = 6 | issue = 20 | pages = L384–L386| doi = 10.1088/0022-3719/6/20/003 |bibcode = 1973JPhC....6L.384A }}</ref>

Working with David Nelson and Marco Ronchetti, Steinhardt formulated mathematical expressions, known as "orientational order parameters", for computing the degree of alignment of interatomic bonds in [[liquids]] and [[solids]] in 1981. Applying them to computer simulations of monatomic supercooled liquids, they showed that the atoms form arrangements with finite-range [[icosahedral]] (soccer-ball like) bond orientational order as liquids cool.

==Honors and awards==
* In 1986, Steinhardt was elected as a Fellow in the [[American Physical Society]] in recognition of his contributions to cosmology and to the theoretical understanding of quasicrystals.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.aps.org/programs/honors/fellowships/archive-all.cfm|title=APS Fellow Archive|website=www.aps.org|access-date=28 January 2019}}</ref>
* In 1994, he was named a Guggenheim Fellow.<ref>{{cite web|url= https://www.gf.org/fellows/all-fellows/paul-j-steinhardt/ |title=Guggenheim Foundation Fellow |work=John Simon Guggenheim Memorial Foundation |access-date=15 September 2019}}</ref>
* In 1998, he was elected to the [[United States National Academy of Sciences]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nasonline.org/directory-entry/paul-j-steinhardt-prchdy/|title=Paul Steinhardt|website=www.nasonline.org|access-date=28 January 2019}}</ref>
* In 2002, Steinhardt was honored for his work on the inflationary model of the universe with the [[Dirac Medal (ICTP)|P.A.M. Dirac Medal]] from the [[International Centre for Theoretical Physics]]. He shared the award with [[Alan Guth]] of MIT and [[Andrei Linde]] of Stanford.<ref name="Dirac Prize"/>
* In 2010, Steinhardt received the [[Oliver E. Buckley Condensed Matter Prize]] of the American Physical Society for his pioneering contributions to the theory of [[quasicrystal]]s.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.aps.org/programs/honors/prizes/prizerecipient.cfm|title=2018 Stanley Corrsin Award Recipient|website=www.aps.org|access-date=28 January 2019}}</ref>
* In 2012, he received the [[John Scott Award]] for his work on quasicrystals.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://garfield.library.upenn.edu/johnscottaward/js2011-2020.html|title=John Scott Award Recipients 2001-2011|website=www.garfield.library.upenn.edu|access-date=28 January 2019|archive-date=4 March 2016|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304201623/http://www.garfield.library.upenn.edu/johnscottaward/js2011-2020.html}}</ref>
* In 2012, Steinhardt was named [[Simons Fellow in Theoretical Physics]]<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.simonsfoundation.org/funding/funding-opportunities/mathematics-physical-sciences/simons-fellow-program/simons-fellows-awardees-theoretical-physics/2012-simons-fellows-awardees-theoretical-physics/ |title=2012 Simons Fellows Awardees: Theoretical Physics &#124; Simons Foundation |access-date=2015-01-06 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150106031109/https://www.simonsfoundation.org/funding/funding-opportunities/mathematics-physical-sciences/simons-fellow-program/simons-fellows-awardees-theoretical-physics/2012-simons-fellows-awardees-theoretical-physics/ |archive-date=2015-01-06 }}</ref> and [[Radcliffe Fellow]] at the [[Radcliffe Institute for Advanced Study]] at Harvard.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.radcliffe.harvard.edu/people/paul-steinhardt|title=Paul Steinhardt|date=7 May 2012|website=Radcliffe Institute for Advanced Study at Harvard University|access-date=28 January 2019}}</ref>
* In 2014, he received the Caltech Distinguished Alumni Award.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.alumni.caltech.edu/distinguished-alumni-awards-2014/|title=Distinguished Alumni Awards|website=Caltech Alumni Association|access-date=28 January 2019|archive-date=3 January 2015|archive-url=https://archive.today/20150103045749/http://www.alumni.caltech.edu/distinguished-alumni-awards-2014/}}</ref>
* In 2014, the [[International Mineralogical Association]] accepted a new mineral from the [[Khatyrka meteorite]] into the official catalogue of natural minerals, and named it "steinhardtite" in his honor.<ref name=steinhardtite/>
* In 2018, he shared the Aspen Institute Italia Award with [[Luca Bindi]] for scientific research and collaboration between Italy and the United States.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.aspeninstitute.it/en/programs/aspen-institute-italia-award-0|title=Aspen Institute Italia Award}}</ref>
* In 2020, he received the [[Niels Bohr Institute]] Medal of Honour.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://nbi.ku.dk/english/about/niels-bohr-institute-honorary-medal/medalje_modtagere/ |title=Niels Bohr Institute, Receivers of the Medal of Honour|date=9 August 2013 }}</ref>
